screens.title: Overview
screens.body:
**Topics covered**

- Who We're Designing For
- Use Real Structure, Not Just Formatting
- Images: Four Kinds
- Color and Contrast
- Readable Text and Links
- Accessible Email
- Word Documents: The Essentials
- PowerPoint: The Essentials
- PDFs, and When to Send Both
- Presenting Accessibly
- Checking Your Work and Getting Help

**Why this matters**

Almost everything we write, send, and present at Benetech is read by someone who may not experience it the way we do: someone who is blind and listens with a screen reader, someone with low vision who enlarges the screen, someone who is deaf or hard of hearing, someone who can't use a mouse. Accessibility means making sure all of them can use what we share.

The good news is that most of it comes down to a handful of habits: using the tools in Word, PowerPoint, and email the way they were designed, describing images, not relying on color alone, and knowing what to send when you aren't sure. This module covers those habits in the places you're most likely to need them. The Word and PowerPoint modules go deeper on each.

Each screen covers one concept: what the problem is, and exactly how to fix it. A short quiz follows once you've been through all of them.

screens.title: Who We're Designing For
screens.body:
People use a wide range of tools to read, listen to, and work with what we share. The most common:

- **Screen readers** read what's on the screen aloud, or send it to a braille display, in the order the file is built.
- **Magnification and larger text** let people with low vision enlarge what they're reading.
- **Captions and transcripts** give people who are deaf or hard of hearing the words in audio and video.
- **Keyboard-only use and voice control** let people who can't use a mouse move through a page or a document.

All of these depend on the same thing: {{answer:general-q1}}how a file is built underneath, not how it looks on the screen{{/answer}}. A heading that is only bold and large looks right to everyone who can see it - but to a screen reader it is just more text.

**Do:** Use the real tools in Word, PowerPoint, and email (heading styles, list buttons, alt text), so the structure is there for any of these tools to use.

**Don't:** Decide something is accessible because it looks tidy. Looks and structure are two different things.

screens.title: Use Real Structure, Not Just Formatting
screens.body:
Most of what makes a file easy to navigate is invisible: headings, lists, and tables that are built with the program's own tools, not drawn by hand.

**Do:**

- {{answer:general-q2}}Make a heading with the built-in Heading style{{/answer}} - Heading 1 for the main title, Heading 2 for main sections, Heading 3 for subsections - in Word, and in Outlook from the **Format text** tab. In PowerPoint, type each slide's title into its Title placeholder.
- Go down one level at a time. Don't jump from Heading 1 straight to Heading 3.
- {{answer:general-q3}}Make a list with the bullet or numbering button{{/answer}}, so the program builds a real list a screen reader can announce ("list of 4 items").
- Use a table only for data, with the header row turned on - never to line things up on the page.

**Don't:** Fake a heading with bold, bigger text, or fake a list by typing a dash, an asterisk, or a number at the start of each line. It looks the same, but it isn't read the same.

screens.title: Images: Four Kinds
screens.body: Not every image needs the same treatment. Before you add or keep an image, ask: what is this image doing here? Almost every image is one of four kinds. ## 1. Regular (informative) images A photo or illustration that adds meaning. Describe what it shows and why it's there, in a sentence or two, in the image's **alt text** (right-click the image and choose **View Alt Text**). Skip "Image of..." - a screen reader already says it's an image. For a logo, use "Logo: Bookshare" (the name of the company or product). The alt text for this picture reads: "A young woman wearing headphones sits on a campus bench, holding a white cane in one hand and a phone showing the Bookshare app in the other. Students walk and talk in the plaza behind her." It says who and what is in the picture and why it matters here, in two sentences, without starting with "Image of". ## 2. Decorative images A divider, a border, or a flourish that adds no information. {{answer:general-q4}}Mark it as decorative{{/answer}} (in the Alt Text pane, check **Mark as decorative**) so screen readers skip it. Don't write a description for it, and don't just leave the alt text blank. The flourish above is a decorative image. It adds nothing a reader needs, so it is marked as decorative, and a screen reader skips it. ## 3. Screenshots A screenshot is a picture of text, and a screen reader can't read the words inside a picture. {{answer:general-q5}}Put the important text or steps shown in the screenshot into the alt text{{/answer}} - the exact wording of an error message, for example. Crop it to the part that matters, and consider typing out the key information instead. The alt text for this screenshot reads: "Screenshot: Document titled "2026 Disability and Inclusion Meetings" with the Navigation pane listing its headings (Date, Participants, Discussion Topics, Minutes) and the Styles pane showing Heading 1 applied to the title." It names the text that matters in the picture - the document's title, its headings, and the style that is applied - so a screen reader user gets the same information a sighted reader takes from it. ## 4. Complex images A chart, graph, diagram, or infographic holds more than a few sentences of alt text can carry. {{answer:general-q6}}Write a short alt text summary and put the full description, or a table of the data, in the text nearby{{/answer}}. The short alt text for this chart reads: "Bar chart: Campus Accessibility Survey Results, 2024 to 2026, for Physical Access, Digital Materials, Support Services, Transportation, and Campus Housing. Every area rose each year, from 44–56% in 2024 to 71–75% in 2026." The longer description goes in the text next to the chart (or in the Notes, or on an appendix slide), where there is room for the details. For this chart it would read: ### Overview A grouped bar chart titled "Campus Accessibility Survey Results." It compares survey results across five campus areas for three years: 2024, 2025, and 2026. Each area has three bars, one per year, and every bar is labeled with its percentage. ### Axes and legend - Vertical axis: percentage, from 0% to 100% in steps of 10%. - Horizontal axis: five campus areas: Physical Access, Digital Materials, Support Services, Transportation, and Campus Housing. - Legend: 2024 is dark blue with diagonal white stripes, 2025 is orange-red with white dots, and 2026 is green with horizontal white stripes. ### Data (as labeled on the chart) | Campus area | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Physical Access | 45% | 60% | 75% | | Digital Materials | 45% | 68% | 75% | | Support Services | 56% | 68% | 75% | | Transportation | 44% | 63% | 72% | | Campus Housing | 45% | 66% | 71% | ### Trends - All five areas improved each year. - In 2024, results were clustered between 44% and 56%. Support Services led, and Transportation was lowest. - The biggest gains came between 2024 and 2025, especially Digital Materials (+23 points) and Campus Housing (+21 points). - Growth slowed between 2025 and 2026, except for Physical Access, which rose another 15 points. - By 2026, all areas were between 71% and 75%. Physical Access, Digital Materials, and Support Services tied at 75%, and Campus Housing was lowest at 71%. **Don't:** Add an image just to fill space, or give every image the same kind of description. The right treatment depends on which of the four it is.

screens.title: Color and Contrast
screens.body:
Color is a good way to add emphasis and make a page easier to look at - as long as nothing depends on color alone.

**Do:**

- {{answer:general-q7}}Pair any meaning carried by color with a second cue, such as a text label, a symbol, or a pattern{{/answer}}. A status shown only as a red, yellow, or green dot is lost to anyone who is colorblind, and a screen reader never announces color at all.
- {{answer:general-q8}}Give normal-size text a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background{{/answer}}. Large text (18 point or bigger, or 14 point bold or bigger) needs at least 3 to 1. Dark text on a light background is the safest choice.
- Check with the **Accessibility Checker**, or with a contrast tool such as [TPGi's Colour Contrast Analyser](https://www.tpgi.com/color-contrast-checker/).

**Don't:** Use light gray text on white, or place text over a busy picture. It can look polished and still be unreadable for people with low vision or color blindness.

screens.title: Readable Text and Links
screens.body:
A few everyday choices make what you write easier for everyone to read, and work better with assistive technology.

**Do:**

- Use a simple sans-serif font, such as Arial, Calibri, or Verdana, at 12 point or larger, and left-align your text.
- Write in plain language: short sentences, and spell out an acronym the first time you use it.
- {{answer:general-q9}}Make link text describe where the link goes{{/answer}} - for example, "Read the 2026 Annual Report". Screen reader users often listen to a list of just the links, so each one has to make sense on its own.
- {{answer:general-q10}}Use paragraph spacing (Spacing Before and After) to make a gap{{/answer}}. A screen reader announces every empty line as "blank". If you ever do need an empty line, never put more than one in a row.

**Don't:** Justify text, write whole sentences in capital letters, or use "click here" or "read more" as a link on its own.

screens.title: Accessible Email
screens.body: Most of us write email every day, and the same rules apply there. A few habits cover most of it. **Do:** - Write a subject line that says what the email is about, so someone scanning or listening to their inbox can tell what it is - {{answer:general-q11}}"Agenda for Thursday's budget review", not "Update" or "Quick question"{{/answer}}. - Put the key information in the body of the message as text, not only in an attachment or a picture. {{answer:general-q12}}If you include a flyer or a screenshot, put what it says in the email as text and add alt text to the image{{/answer}}. - Use bullets, numbered lists, and (in a long message) headings from the **Format text** tab, instead of typing dashes and spacing. - Make link text descriptive, and write out email addresses and phone numbers as text. - Keep your signature accessible: contact details as text, and a logo with alt text ("Logo: Benetech"), never a single image of your whole signature. - For a long or important message, run **Review > Check Accessibility** before you send. Here is an email with a real heading chosen from the **Styles** menu on the **Format text** tab: The alt text for this screenshot reads: "Microsoft Outlook screenshot: Draft titled "Accessible Email Message" with the Styles menu open and Heading 1 selected. The body has a "Main Topic" heading, normal text, a bulleted list, and Charles LaPierre's Benetech signature." **Don't:** Send an email that is only an image, use all capital letters or long strings of emoji, or rely on color or bold alone to show what matters. Attachments follow the same rules as any other file - see the PDF screen for more.

screens.title: Word Documents: The Essentials
screens.body:
A Word document is the file most of us make most often, and the habits are the same ones you've already seen in this module.

**Do:**

- Use the built-in **Heading** styles for headings, and the bullet and numbering buttons for lists.
- Add alt text to each meaningful image (right-click > **View Alt Text**), and mark purely decorative ones as decorative.
- Make link text describe the destination.
- Use a sans-serif font at 12 point or larger, left-aligned, with spacing set in **Paragraph** instead of extra empty lines.
- For a table, turn on the **Header Row** and keep the table simple.
- Finish by running **Review > Check Accessibility** and fixing what it reports.

**Don't:** Use the Title style for your document's title. Use Heading 1 instead - screen readers announce Heading 1 as a heading, but not Title.

The Word modules go through each of these in detail, with shortcuts for both PC and Mac.

screens.title: PowerPoint: The Essentials
screens.body:
A slide deck is read by screen readers slide by slide, so it needs a little more care than a document.

**Do:**

- {{answer:general-q13}}Give every slide a unique title typed into the Title placeholder{{/answer}}. Choose a layout that has one. A text box that only looks like a title isn't announced as one.
- Check the reading order on each slide (**Review > Reading Order** on Windows). It is the order a screen reader reads things in, and it does not automatically match the order you see.
- Add alt text to meaningful images and mark decorative ones as decorative.
- Keep slides short - about six bullets of a few words each - and split a crowded slide in two rather than shrinking the text.
- Make sure every video has captions.
- Finish with **Review > Check Accessibility**.

**Don't:** Repeat the same title on several slides, or put the only copy of important information in a picture. The PowerPoint modules cover each of these in detail.

screens.title: PDFs, and When to Send Both
screens.body:
A PDF only carries over what is already in the file it came from, and how you create it matters.

**Do:**

- Fix the Word or PowerPoint file first, then create the PDF from it. {{answer:general-q14}}Use Save As or Export with the option that keeps accessibility tags{{/answer}}: on a PC, **File > Export > Create PDF/XPS**, then **Options**, and check **Document structure tags for accessibility**; on a Mac, **Save As** PDF and choose **Best for electronic distribution and accessibility**.
- {{answer:general-q15}}If you aren't certain a PDF is accessible, send the original Word or PowerPoint file along with it{{/answer}}, and say so in your message: "A PDF and an editable version are attached." The original is usually the more accessible of the two, people can choose the version that works best for them, and it gives someone the chance to fix anything that is missing.

**Don't:**

- Use **Print** to make a PDF. Printing strips out the headings, lists, and alt text you built in.
- Scan a paper page and send the scan on its own. A scan is a picture of text, which a screen reader can't read.

screens.title: Presenting Accessibly
screens.body:
An accessible slide file is only half of an accessible presentation. How you present it matters just as much, especially for anyone following by listening.

**Do:**

- {{answer:general-q16}}Describe what's on the screen out loud, including the key text and what you're pointing at{{/answer}} - if someone could only hear you, what would they need to know?
- Say "next slide" or give the slide number as you move on.
- Share the slides, in an accessible format, before the session and not only afterward.
- Turn on live captions in your meeting tool, speak at a steady pace, and pause so captioners and interpreters can keep up.
- Say your name before you speak in a meeting, and read questions from the chat out loud.

**Don't:** Say "as you can see here" and point, or treat the slide as if it carries the whole message. What you say is part of the presentation, not an extra.

screens.title: Checking Your Work and Getting Help
screens.body:
The last step is always to check. Word, PowerPoint, and Outlook all have an **Accessibility Checker** under the **Review** tab.

It catches a lot - missing alt text, low contrast, missing slide titles - but it isn't the whole job. {{answer:general-q17}}After it reports no problems, read through the file yourself{{/answer}}, because it can't tell whether your alt text is actually meaningful, or whether you used color to carry meaning.

**A few quick checks to add:**

- In Word, open the **Navigation Pane** (**View > Navigation Pane**). If your headings are real, they appear there as an outline of the document.
- In Word, try **Review > Read Aloud** and listen to a page. You'll hear what a screen reader user hears.
- Zoom in to 200 percent and make sure everything is still readable.

**When you're not sure:** send both the PDF and the original file, and ask your manager or Benetech's accessibility team before you send.

**Don't:** Treat a clean Checker result as the finish line.
